**Proof.**

Since $\lim_{x\to+\infty}\frac{f(x)}{x}=0$, for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $M>0$ such that for all $x\ge M$,
$$\left|\frac{f(x)}{x}\right|<\varepsilon,\quad\text{i.e.}\quad |f(x)|<\varepsilon x.$$

For each positive integer $n$ with $n\ge M$, apply the Mean Value Theorem to $f$ on the interval $[n,2n]$. Since $f$ is differentiable on $(0,+\infty)$, it is continuous on $[n,2n]$ and differentiable on $(n,2n)$, so there exists $x_n\in(n,2n)$ such that
$$f'(x_n)=\frac{f(2n)-f(n)}{2n-n}=\frac{f(2n)-f(n)}{n}.$$

We estimate:
$$|f'(x_n)|=\left|\frac{f(2n)-f(n)}{n}\right|\le\frac{|f(2n)|+|f(n)|}{n}.$$

Since $n\ge M$ implies $2n\ge M$, we have $|f(2n)|<\varepsilon\cdot 2n$ and $|f(n)|<\varepsilon\cdot n$. Therefore
$$|f'(x_n)|<\frac{2\varepsilon n+\varepsilon n}{n}=3\varepsilon.$$

Since $x_n\in(n,2n)$, we have $x_n\to+\infty$ as $n\to\infty$. The above shows that for every $\varepsilon>0$, there exists $N$ (any $N\ge M$) such that for all $n\ge N$, $|f'(x_n)|<3\varepsilon$. Since $\varepsilon>0$ was arbitrary,
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}f'(x_n)=0.$$

Thus $\{x_n\}$ is the desired sequence with $x_n\to\infty$ and $f'(x_n)\to 0$. $\blacksquare$
